I'm not sure how many people have been sued by MS over that trying to make an OS compatible with Windows because the executable formats are all proprietary. Apple (I think) does the exact same thing.

Because Windows is a tremendously complicated program that actually consists of hundreds of programs and millions upon millions of lines of code, assembled by thousands of people and probably having taken several tens of thousands of man-years to write.

The product of this must be capable, at the level of machine code, of emulating every way in which the Windows operating system interacts with programs written to its API, including both documented and undocumented behavior, precisely constructing and/or reconstructing the environment in which the program expects to run. Additionally it must do this for multiple versions of Windows at once, and be capable of maintaining significant amounts of backwards compatibility, both with itself and with Windows. The programming interfaces, many of which may be undocumented, consist of many thousands of different routines and data structures, as well as auxiliary system services that may or may not in fact be used by any particular Windows program but are necessary to ensure Windows compatibility. It must do this in the constraints of another operating system and operating environment, with sufficient interaction between processes so that multiple programs running under the same emulation system may work together. In the case of a non-x86 or non-AMD64 architecture it must then be capable of emulating one or both of these machine languages. This only gets more complicated if you add in the driver system, as well as other aspects such as the layout of data structures, memory allocation patterns, etc., in no small part because programmers don't always do what is considered the right thing (never mind that the 'right thing' can change, is not necessarily universally agreed on, and in some cases may just be plain impossible to do with the tools given). Additionally all of this has to work together with correct timing and work together correctly in a variety of other ways, and may in fact not only have to be feature-for-feature compatible, but bug-for-bug compatibility in order to account for undocumented quirks and/or corresponding workarounds. Other architecture-specific behaviors must be accurately emulated as well, e.g. library interfaces so you can operate with DLLs, particularly those that cannot be replicated by your system for whatever reason. Other system services must also be provided, such as scheduling, IPC, threading, settings management (e.g. the Registry). This must all be done without any reference to the original source code - and for legal reasons they can't include code written (or perhaps by advice given) by anyone who has ever had any significant exposure to or experience with the source code of Windows, or its many, many parts. This has to be done with what amounts to a moving target that is constantly being patched, upgraded, updated, or having additional parts thrown in. And all of this is just off the top of my head.

Add into this the fact that Microsoft can and will try to destroy your project, as well as the fact that most of your programmers are going to be volunteers working on their own time, and you've got yourself a recipe for a royal mess, to say the least. The fact that Wine and ReactOS have gotten as far as they have is nothing short of astounding. And, truth be told, I doubt either will ever be complete, if for nothing else than the fact that Windows is, as stated, very much a moving target, and even moreso now that Windows 10 is fixated on the idea of a rolling release.

It gets a little easier if you've got the source code and want something roughly compatible for quick ports, and such libraries have in fact existed at least at a few points in Windows' history (I remember a commercial product that cost an arm and a leg that reimplemented the basic Win32 API library for Unix). It also gets easier if you're able to reuse parts of the core Windows systems, which is something that has been done by other systems as well, such as Sun's long-dead Wabi (which fulfilled a function similar to Wine, but only for a fairly well-defined set of business applications, and pretty expensively at that), and I think there are, or at least used to be, options for Wine to do that to increase reliability and performance. But ultimately, because it is really, really, really, REALLY hard. You aren't just implementing the API for an operating system, you are implementing an entire environment and all its interactions, abilities, and even flaws.
